clinicalPearls: Os acromiale is failure of fusion of one or more acromial ossification centres, which normally unite in early adult life.
It is frequently an incidental, asymptomatic finding and is bilateral in a substantial proportion of affected individuals.
Classified by the site of the unfused segment: pre-acromion, meso-acromion, meta-acromion and basi-acromion, with the meso-acromion type being the most common and most often symptomatic.
An axillary lateral radiograph is the key view; on a standard anteroposterior film the ossicle can be mistaken for the acromioclavicular joint or missed entirely.
A mobile fragment can be pulled inferiorly by the deltoid during contraction, dynamically narrowing the subacromial space and producing secondary impingement.
It is associated with rotator cuff pathology, and both should be assessed together when planning treatment.
Do not confuse an os acromiale with an acute acromial fracture; smooth, corticated, symmetrical margins favour the congenital ossicle.
Caution is needed at arthroscopic subacromial decompression, as aggressive resection of an unstable fragment can destabilise the deltoid origin.
reference.pathophysiology: The acromion develops from several ossification centres that typically coalesce by the third decade. Os acromiale results when one or more of these centres fails to fuse, leaving a segment joined to the remaining acromion by fibrocartilaginous or fibrous tissue rather than bone. Symptoms arise when this synchondrosis becomes mobile or degenerate: motion at the pseudarthrosis generates pain, and traction by the deltoid, whose fibres insert on the mobile fragment, can tilt it inferiorly to reduce the subacromial outlet and cause dynamic impingement of the underlying cuff. Chronic instability of the segment may also provoke reactive changes at the synchondrosis and contribute to adjacent rotator cuff tendinopathy or tearing.
additionalDifferentials: Subacromial impingement syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Axillary lateral radiograph to demonstrate and classify the unfused segment
Outlet (scapular Y) and anteroposterior views to assess the subacromial arch
CT to define fragment size, bony margins and any degenerative change at the synchondrosis
MRI to evaluate the rotator cuff, marrow oedema across the synchondrosis and bursal changes
Diagnostic local anaesthetic injection into the synchondrosis to confirm it as the pain source
Dynamic ultrasound to assess fragment mobility and cuff integrity
redFlags: Acute onset after trauma with sharp margins suggesting a true acromial fracture rather than a congenital ossicle
Progressive rotator cuff weakness indicating a significant associated tear
Marrow oedema with destructive change raising concern for infection or tumour
Deltoid dysfunction following prior surgery to the region
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic os acromiale requires no treatment and carries an excellent prognosis. Symptomatic cases often respond to conservative management, while persistent instability may require fixation with bone grafting or fragment excision, with outcomes influenced by fragment size and the state of the associated rotator cuff.
pitfalls: Missing the ossicle by omitting an axillary lateral view or misreading it as the acromioclavicular joint.
Mistaking a congenital os acromiale for an acute fracture and vice versa.
Performing standard acromioplasty that destabilises the fragment and deltoid origin without addressing the synchondrosis.
Failing to recognise and treat a coexisting rotator cuff tear.
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
management: Reassurance and no intervention for the common incidental, asymptomatic os acromiale
Initial conservative management with activity modification, physiotherapy targeting rotator cuff and scapular stabiliser strengthening, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Image-guided subacromial or intra-synchondrosis corticosteroid injection for symptomatic impingement, which also helps confirm the pain source
Excision of a small unstable pre-acromion fragment, or open reduction and internal fixation with bone grafting for a larger mobile meso-acromion, when conservative care fails
Concurrent assessment and repair of any associated rotator cuff tear, with subacromial decompression, at the time of surgery
Referral to a shoulder surgeon for persistent instability, with fragment size and cuff status guiding the operative choice
